title: Check yourself: class and object introspection

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A code generator writes one builder method for each element of Account.class.getDeclaredMethods(). Account declares open, deposit, withdraw and close, in that order. On a developer laptop the generated file always lists deposit, close, open, withdraw. CI runs the same JDK version in a container with different JVM flags. What should the team expect from the file generated in CI?

options.text: The laptop's order, since the JVM keeps the methods in the order the class file stores them
options.says: neither run on the page followed the source order, and the javadoc puts the elements in no particular order

options.text: The laptop's order, since the JVM sorts them the same way for any one JDK version
options.says: the page's two runs used one JDK 21 build and still disagreed; a flag such as -Xshare:off was enough

options.text: An order that may differ from the laptop's, since the JVM sorts them by where each name sits in its memory
options.says: the order is unspecified and in HotSpot follows where method names sit in memory, which JVM settings change

options.text: An order that may differ from the laptop's, since a JVM in a container sorts them by name
options.says: no JVM setting sorts them; neither run on the page was alphabetical, and code that needs an order sorts the result itself

origin.section: Reflection Returns Members in No Particular Order

questions.stem: A validation tool must call every method annotated @Check on a Customer object. One of them is a protected method declared in Customer's abstract superclass Party, and Customer does not override it. Which lookup finds it?

options.text: getMethods() on Customer alone, since that call includes the methods a class inherits
options.says: getMethods() includes inherited methods but only public ones, so the protected method is missing

options.text: getDeclaredMethods() on Customer alone, since that call includes methods of every access level
options.says: getDeclaredMethods() lists every access level but only the class's own declarations, not Party's

options.text: getMethods() on Customer and then on Party, since each call adds the methods of one more class
options.says: getMethods() never lists a protected method, on Party or anywhere else

options.text: getDeclaredMethods() on Customer and then on Party, since each call adds the methods of one more class
options.says: walking up getSuperclass() with getDeclaredMethods() sees every access level of every class in the chain

origin.section: getMethods and getDeclaredMethods Answer Different Questions, and Neither Lists Everything

questions.stem: A web framework turns every method annotated @Post in a controller class into a route keyed by method name. AccountController implements Controller<AccountRequest> and declares a single method, @Post public void handle(AccountRequest r), which overrides Controller<T>'s handle(T). At startup the framework fails with "two routes named handle". Where does the second one come from?

options.text: A handle(Object) in AccountController's class file that javac generated, which carries the @Post annotation as well
options.says: the override needs a bridge method taking the erased type; javac adds it to the class and copies the annotations onto it

options.text: A handle(Object) in AccountController's class file that the JVM copies from the interface, which carries the @Post annotation as well
options.says: nothing is copied from the interface at run time; the extra method is in the class file because the compiler wrote it there

options.text: The interface's own abstract handle(T), which the framework sees next to the override, since interface methods are part of the controller's methods
options.says: the second method is declared by AccountController itself and is reported as a bridge, not the interface's abstract method

options.text: The interface's own abstract handle(T), which the framework sees next to the override, since an override passes its annotations up to the method it overrides
options.says: annotations go from the method onto the compiler's bridge in the same class, not up to the interface

origin.section: The Compiler Adds Methods You Never Wrote: Bridges and Lambda Bodies

questions.stem: Shape is sealed and permits Circle and Polygon; Polygon is sealed and permits Triangle and Quad. One service node is deployed without the jar that holds Quad. What does Polygon.class.getPermittedSubclasses() return on that node?

options.text: Triangle and Quad, since the permitted names are stored in Polygon's own class file
options.says: the call returns Class objects, and a permitted class that cannot be loaded is left out

options.text: Triangle alone, since a permitted class that cannot be loaded is left out of the result
options.says: the javadoc says such a class is silently ignored; with Quad.class removed the call returned only Triangle

options.text: No array but an error, since a permitted class that cannot be loaded makes the call fail
options.says: the call does not throw for a missing permitted class; it shrinks the result

options.text: No array but null, since Polygon's sealed hierarchy can no longer be completed
options.says: null means the type is not sealed; Polygon is still sealed, so the result is an array

origin.section: Read a Record Through Its Components and a Sealed Type Through Its Permitted Subclasses

questions.stem: A cache holds values as Object. A debug endpoint wants to show the element type of a value that is a list, with only the value in hand, and calls value.getClass().getGenericSuperclass(). The value came from new ArrayList<Instant>(). What does the endpoint show?

options.text: java.util.AbstractList<E>, since the call reports what the class declares rather than what the object was given
options.says: getGenericSuperclass() reports what the class declares, and ArrayList declares AbstractList<E>; the object keeps no type argument

options.text: java.util.AbstractList<java.time.Instant>, since the call reports what the object was given rather than what the class declares
options.says: type arguments are erased from objects; an ArrayList<Instant> has the same Class as any other ArrayList

options.text: java.util.ArrayList<java.time.Instant>, since the call reports the object's own type together with its arguments
options.says: the call returns the superclass as the class declares it, and no object carries its type arguments

options.text: java.util.ArrayList<E>, since the call reports the class's own type together with its type variable
options.says: the call returns the declared superclass, AbstractList<E>, not the class itself

origin.section: Type Arguments Survive in Declarations, Not in Objects

concepts: An object keeps no type arguments: an ArrayList<String> has the same Class as any ArrayList, and getGenericSuperclass() on it gives the class's declaration, AbstractList<E>.
getDeclaredMethods() and getMethods() return members in no specified order, and the order changes with JVM setup even for the same class file and JDK.
A permitted subclass that cannot be loaded is silently left out of getPermittedSubclasses().
